subtopics.title: Physical and chemical properties

slots.X: A copper strip, graphite sheet and crystalline salt all transmit current in at least one tested state. Copper conducts when solid, graphite much better along the sheet than across stacked layers, and salt only after melting. Explain the different carrier mechanisms and why an identical current reading is not evidence of identical bonding.
slots.Y: Conductivity is a macroscopic response; a mechanism must identify a mobile charge carrier and the structure permitting its motion. Direction and physical state help discriminate the models.
slots.Z: Copper: mobile electrons through metallic structure. Graphite: delocalised electrons within covalent layers, anisotropic transport. Salt: ions fixed in ordinary lattice, mobile after melting. Equal readings can arise from distinct carrier types and depend on sample geometry and contacts. The shared observable is charge transport, not bond identity.
slots.W: Connect three distinct microscopic carrier mechanisms to state/direction evidence and reject the equal-current inference.

qrt_instances.replacement_rule: Conductivity is a macroscopic response; a mechanism must identify a mobile charge carrier and the structure permitting its motion. Direction and physical state help discriminate the models.

qrt_instances.independent_check: Could a dry salt conduct weakly through defects? Explain why this would not automatically establish metallic bonding. Yes, defects can permit ionic motion in some solids. Carrier identity requires independent evidence, not a binary conductivity test.

slots.X: A black solid P conducts along its flat faces but weakly across stacked layers; Q is shiny and conducts in all three measured directions; R is nonconducting when solid but its melt conducts. Assign plausible bonding models, identify which assignments are nonunique and propose independent tests.
slots.Y: Mobile charge carriers may be electrons or ions; graphite is a nonmetal with anisotropic electronic conduction. Ionic lattices usually have immobile ions; dissolved or molten ions may carry current. Conductivity alone cannot identify a material; control contacts, geometry and phase.
slots.Z: P fits layered graphite with delocalised electrons preferentially moving within layers. Q fits metallic electron conduction but lustre/conductivity do not prove metallic identity. R fits mobile ions in a melt; composition must confirm ionic bonding. Control geometry and contacts; obtain composition/structural evidence for each.
slots.W: Compare carrier models, directional and phase evidence, and distinguish consistency from identification.

qrt_instances.student_task: A black solid P conducts along its flat faces but weakly across stacked layers; Q is shiny and conducts in all three measured directions; R is nonconducting when solid but its melt conducts. Assign plausible bonding models, identify which assignments are nonunique and propose independent tests.
qrt_instances.wrong_idea: Single conductivity observation proves metallic or ionic bonding.
qrt_instances.replacement_rule: Mobile charge carriers may be electrons or ions; graphite is a nonmetal with anisotropic electronic conduction. Ionic lattices usually have immobile ions; dissolved or molten ions may carry current. Conductivity alone cannot identify a material; control contacts, geometry and phase.
qrt_instances.visual_job: Build an observation, species or structural ledger appropriate to this exact task without marking the decisive result.
qrt_instances.independent_check: If a molecular solid produces conducting solution, does that establish that the original solid is ionic? No; molecular substances can ionise or react with water. Solution carriers do not establish original bonding.

slots.X: In a hypothetical survey, dry X and dry Y are electrical insulators. X dissolves to yield equal amounts of positive and negative monovalent ions and conducts; Y reacts with water to yield equal amounts of ions and also conducts. A report identifies both original solids as ionic because the solutions have the same ion concentration. Combine the particle and experimental evidence to evaluate this conclusion and propose a way to distinguish the initial materials.
slots.Y: The same final species can result from dissociation or chemical ionisation. A state change, dissolution and reaction are distinct processes; a final measurement does not always reconstruct initial identity.
slots.Z: Both final liquids have mobile ions; X may be an ionic solid whose pre-existing ions separate, while Y may be molecular and form ions by reaction with water. The equal concentrations do not determine original structures or identical conductivity (mobility matters). Distinguish initial solid by structural/composition evidence or a suitable nonreactive-solvent/melt test where feasible. Do not infer initial bonding solely from final ions.
slots.W: Integrate before/after species inventories and independent solid evidence, explaining the underdetermination.

subtopics.title: Metal reactivity and displacement

slots.X: A clean iron strip is immersed in a Cu²⁺ solution. In a simplified record 0.040 mol Fe²⁺ forms, 0.030 mol Cu is recovered and no other products are measured. Explain how the two half-reactions couple, whether the recorded copper amount accounts for all electron transfer, and why the blue colour fading alone is insufficient.
slots.Y: In a sole displacement reaction, oxidation and reduction are coupled by electron conservation. Product recovery is not necessarily reaction extent; colour is qualitative evidence.
slots.Z: Fe→Fe²⁺+2e⁻ supplies 0.080 mol electrons; Cu²⁺+2e⁻→Cu consumes 0.060 mol. 0.020 mol electrons unaccounted if measurements exact. Incomplete Cu recovery, another electron acceptor or measurement error are alternatives; colour changes alone do not identify or quantify products. Sulfate is spectator if present.
slots.W: Explain coupled electron transfer and independently reconcile the observed species amounts.

qrt_instances.student_task: A clean iron strip is immersed in a Cu²⁺ solution. In a simplified record 0.040 mol Fe²⁺ forms, 0.030 mol Cu is recovered and no other products are measured. Explain how the two half-reactions couple, whether the recorded copper amount accounts for all electron transfer, and why the blue colour fading alone is insufficient.
qrt_instances.wrong_idea: Displacement is only an exchange of names and all metal mole ratios must match.
qrt_instances.replacement_rule: In a sole displacement reaction, oxidation and reduction are coupled by electron conservation. Product recovery is not necessarily reaction extent; colour is qualitative evidence.
qrt_instances.visual_job: Learner constructs the task-specific representation in protected W; no completed representation before attempt.
qrt_instances.independent_check: If Fe instead forms Fe³⁺ and Cu is the sole acceptor, how much Cu is formed per 0.020 mol Fe? 0.060 mol e⁻ /2=0.030 mol Cu.

slots.X: Clean A displaces B²⁺; clean B displaces C²⁺; clean D displaces B²⁺. A coated D strip gives no deposit in A²⁺. Draw the supported partial order, list unresolved pairs, and choose the smallest additional controlled comparison needed to decide the most reactive metal.
slots.Y: Comparable positive displacement tests constrain relative tendencies; transitivity assumes the same relevant chemical system. Negative tests require control for passivation and sensitivity.
slots.Z: Edges A>B, B>C, D>B; transitivity gives A>C and D>C under comparable conditions. A vs D unresolved; coated negative does not resolve it. These are the two possible maximal metals. A controlled clean A/D comparison with suitable verification can decide which is above; reciprocal test if negative is ambiguous. No ranking of rates.
slots.W: Select a partial-order graph and identify the missing edge controlling the maximal element.

qrt_instances.wrong_idea: One negative coated test completes a reactivity series.
qrt_instances.replacement_rule: Comparable positive displacement tests constrain relative tendencies; transitivity assumes the same relevant chemical system. Negative tests require control for passivation and sensitivity.

slots.X: Clean P displaces Q²⁺ and clean R displaces Q²⁺ in matched conditions. Coated P does not visibly react with R²⁺. Separately 0.030 mol P dissolves as P²⁺ while 0.020 mol Q deposits. Infer partial order, test whether sole displacement explains amounts and propose controls.
slots.Y: Positive displacement indicates relative tendency under controlled conditions; negative evidence may be masked by coating or kinetics. For a sole coupled reaction, electron release equals electron uptake. Divalent-to-divalent displacement gives equal amounts only if no other electron acceptor or measurement loss.
slots.Z: P>Q, R>Q; P versus R unresolved. P→P²⁺+2e⁻ gives 0.060 mol e⁻; Q²⁺+2e⁻→Q consumes 0.040 mol. Sole reaction requires equal moles, so 0.020 mol e⁻ unaccounted; check side reduction, incomplete collection, measurement. Compare cleaned reciprocal P/R tests.
slots.W: Combine partial order and electron ledger, reject inconsistent single-reaction account.

subtopics.title: Ionic compound formation and properties

slots.X: An ideal salt L contains L²⁺ and X⁻. A dry crystal gives negligible current; molten sample conducts; aqueous solution of the same nominal mass gives lower current than a more dilute solution of a different salt. Explain all three observations without claiming that nominal mass or ion count alone controls conductivity.
slots.Y: Ionic neutrality determines formula ratio; transport depends on charged species mobility, concentration and charge. Equal sample mass need not imply equal formula amount.
slots.Z: LX₂ formula neutral; ions in ordinary crystal confined, mobile in melt. Dissolved ions are mobile but different salts may differ in actual concentration, degree of dissociation, carrier charge/mobility, temperature and geometry. Nominal mass not number of ions. Compare matched geometry/temperature, concentration and species before ranking.
slots.W: Explain phase-dependent transport and distinguish nominal amount from carrier mobility and concentration.

slots.Y: A formula unit gives smallest charge-neutral integer ratio. A dissolved or molten salt may conduct through mobile ions, with conductivity depending on charge, concentration and mobility. Counts based on complete dissociation are model predictions.
slots.Z: AX₃ and BY are neutral. AX₃ produces 0.080 mol ions; BY 0.040 mol. Conductivity also depends on charge, mobility and interactions, so count alone cannot rank it. Ordinary dry ionic lattices have largely fixed ions; solid electrolytes are exceptions.

subtopics.title: Extraction and basic metallurgical processes

slots.X: A proposal treats two hypothetical oxide feeds M₂O and NO identically with carbon because both equations can be balanced. M is sodium-like and N zinc-like. Explain why balanced stoichiometry is necessary but insufficient, compare plausible extraction mechanisms and identify what additional evidence is required before predicting actual recovery.
slots.Y: Metal extraction requires a chemically feasible reduction or external electrical work; actual recovery also depends on separation. Balanced equations cannot by themselves establish feasibility.
slots.Z: Atom balance describes amounts, not thermodynamic feasibility or rates. Highly reactive M typically needs electrolysis of a suitable molten salt; less reactive N oxide may be reduced by carbon/CO in appropriate conditions. Electrolysis supplies external electrical energy; chemical reduction transfers electrons from reductant. Need oxide stability/conditions, separation, side reaction and recovery evidence. No practical procedure implied.
slots.W: Explain difference between formal balance, energetic feasibility and recovery for two ore models.

subtopics.title: Oxides and amphoterism

slots.X: Two pure white oxides X and Y both react with acid; only X forms a soluble anionic hydroxo species in strong aqueous base. Explain the difference using ZnO as a model for X and MgO for Y. Write the appropriate acid and base equations, and explain why using excess base rather than weak alkali matters.
slots.Y: An amphoteric oxide can act as base toward acid and react with strong base to form soluble species; the two contexts require different products and balanced equations.
slots.Z: ZnO+2H⁺→Zn²⁺+H₂O; ZnO+2OH⁻+H₂O→[Zn(OH)₄]²⁻. MgO+2H⁺→Mg²⁺+H₂O; no analogous simple strong-base dissolution expected under stated ordinary model. Amphoterism requires both reagent contexts, sufficient conditions and product evidence; a negative weak-base observation is insufficient.
slots.W: Explain two acid/base mechanisms through phase-appropriate species and evidence.

qrt_instances.student_task: Two pure white oxides X and Y both react with acid; only X forms a soluble anionic hydroxo species in strong aqueous base. Explain the difference using ZnO as a model for X and MgO for Y. Write the appropriate acid and base equations, and explain why using excess base rather than weak alkali matters.
qrt_instances.wrong_idea: All oxides dissolving in acid are amphoteric.
qrt_instances.replacement_rule: An amphoteric oxide can act as base toward acid and react with strong base to form soluble species; the two contexts require different products and balanced equations.

slots.Z: M₂O₃+6H⁺→2M³⁺+3H₂O. Oxide amount 0.020 mol; molar mass 102; 2M+48=102 gives M=27, consistent with Al. Base: M₂O₃+2OH⁻+3H₂O→2[M(OH)₄]⁻. Atom and charge conserved. Acid response also fits basic oxide; need base/product evidence.
slots.W: Infer oxide identity and balance phase-specific ionic reactions; distinguish dual evidence.

subtopics.title: Corrosion and prevention

slots.X: In matched iron coupons, A is wet and oxygenated, B is wet and deoxygenated, C is dry with oxygen, and D is wet and oxygenated but has poor ionic conductivity. Explain why electron transfer requires two coupled processes and predict which comparison isolates oxygen, moisture and ionic transport; distinguish observation from guaranteed rate.
slots.Y: Corrosion couples electron movement in metal to ionic movement in electrolyte; oxygen reduction is a common cathodic reaction. A controlled experiment changes one relevant variable at a time.
slots.Z: A vs B tests oxygen; A vs C tests moisture if other conditions matched; A vs D tests ionic transport. Fe oxidation releases electrons, oxygen reduction consumes them in ordinary neutral aerated rusting; water enables ionic transport. D may corrode more slowly but exact rate needs measurements. Other acceptors can enable corrosion without oxygen.
slots.W: Connect local half-reactions to three controlled comparisons and limit rate prediction.

qrt_instances.student_task: In matched iron coupons, A is wet and oxygenated, B is wet and deoxygenated, C is dry with oxygen, and D is wet and oxygenated but has poor ionic conductivity. Explain why electron transfer requires two coupled processes and predict which comparison isolates oxygen, moisture and ionic transport; distinguish observation from guaranteed rate.
qrt_instances.wrong_idea: Oxygen or moisture alone guarantees a specific rusting rate.
qrt_instances.replacement_rule: Corrosion couples electron movement in metal to ionic movement in electrolyte; oxygen reduction is a common cathodic reaction. A controlled experiment changes one relevant variable at a time.

qrt_instances.independent_check: Can oxygen-free acidic water corrode iron through a different cathodic reaction? Yes; H⁺ reduction can be a cathodic process under suitable conditions, so no oxygen does not mean all corrosion impossible.

slots.X: Bare iron, painted iron with a scratch, iron joined electrically to zinc with a scratch, and iron separated electrically from zinc are in matched wet oxygenated conditions. Select a mechanism for each, predict which can retain protection at a scratch and identify a measurement distinguishing a physical barrier from sacrificial protection.
slots.Y: A protective coating can block reactants or alter electrochemical reactions. Sacrificial protection needs electronic connection, an electrolyte and sufficient sacrificial material.
slots.Z: Bare iron accessible; paint is barrier and scratch exposes iron. Connected zinc can oxidise preferentially and deliver electrons to exposed iron via contact, with ionic path, while separated zinc cannot provide galvanic protection. Compare equal exposed area and measure zinc loss/electrical contact or potential; exact corrosion rates not implied.
slots.W: Choose barrier vs galvanic mechanism and predict contact-dependence.

slots.X: Matched iron coupons show negligible rust in dry air, some in aerated fresh water, more in aerated salt water, much less in deoxygenated salt water. Scratched zinc-coated iron corrodes less than bare iron in aerated salt water. Explain the pattern with oxidation/reduction, distinguish salt from oxygen and propose a coating control.
slots.Y: Corrosion couples metal oxidation with reduction of an electron acceptor; ions carry charge through water. Salt accelerates many conditions but cannot replace oxygen in ordinary rusting. Sacrificial protection depends on electronic contact and ionic path.
slots.Z: Fe→Fe²⁺+2e⁻; in aerated neutral water O₂+2H₂O+4e⁻→4OH⁻. Water electrolyte, salt often increases ionic conductivity; oxygen accepts electrons. Zinc preferentially oxidises when electrically connected; paint mainly blocks access. Control exposed iron area, contact, oxygen. Rust products vary, not one pure phase.
slots.W: Reconcile controlled observations with electrochemical mechanism and protection requirements.
